rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: There are 45 threads because numbering zero through 44 includes both endpoints. Each CUDA warp has 32 lanes, so threads 0–31 fill the first warp, and threads 32–44 occupy 44 − 32 + 1 = 13 lanes in the second. That gives 2 warps, with 13 active lanes in the last warp and 19 unused lanes.

rows.name: context-16-frozen-16
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Because a timeout means the client does not know whether the charge succeeded—not that it failed. Retrying with the same durable idempotency key lets the server recognize the same operation and return its saved result, while atomic key ownership prevents concurrent retries from charging twice. The charge and its durable outcome must commit atomically; otherwise, a crash between charging and saving the result leaves a gap where a retry could charge again. If the charge happens at an external payment provider, a local database transaction alone cannot guarantee this: the provider must support idempotency with a stable key, or an equivalent recovery protocol must resolve the original charge before retrying.

review.note: Unknown timeout outcome needs stable durable key and atomic ownership/outcome. External provider charge correctly requires provider idempotency/reconciliation; no invented local-transaction guarantee.

rows.answer: Because compare-and-swap applies your update only if the current value matches your expectation; keeping an obsolete expectation can cause repeated failures, and keeping a stale desired value can overwrite intervening progress. For an increment, if you expected 5 but the failed attempt observes 7, retry expecting 7 and proposing 8—not 6. rows.name: context-27-frozen-27
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: A circular buffer is a good fit because it provides fixed capacity and constant-time FIFO push and pop without shifting elements. With 17 slots, track a head index and an element count: reject push when the count is 17, fail pop when it is zero, insert at `(head + count) % 17`, and advance the head after a successful pop. The count distinguishes full from empty while allowing all 17 slots to be used. The requested tests check empty-pop failure, overflow rejection without changing existing contents, FIFO ordering, and correct indexing when the buffer wraps around.

rows.name: context-30-frozen-30
rows.question: Why?
rows.answer: Atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing; it does not prevent concurrent transactions from making decisions from stale snapshots. Start with Alice and Bob both on call: transaction A reads both rows, checks that Bob is on call, and takes Alice off call; transaction B reads the same initial snapshot, checks that Alice is on call, and takes Bob off call. Under snapshot isolation, they write different rows, so both can commit, leaving neither on call—even though each read-check-write operation was one atomic transaction. No serial execution could produce that result: the second transaction would see only one person remaining and refuse to remove them. Preventing this write skew requires serializable isolation or coordination that forces these transactions to conflict, such as updating a shared guard row within each transaction.
